hooks.text: A spacecraft once found strange, linear scars carved into a deep-space rock.
Why did a tiny asteroid share the same mysterious grooves as a moon?
A distant rock was just a point of light until an explorer arrived.

title: Scars on a Deep-Space Rock
description: NASA's Galileo probe made history as the first spacecraft to visit an asteroid, revealing mysterious surface features on 951 Gaspra.

beats.text: A spacecraft once found strange, linear scars carved into a deep-space rock.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of Galileo spacecraft flying past asteroid 951 Gaspra.

beats.text: In 1991, NASA’s Galileo spacecraft approached the asteroid 951 Gaspra while traveling toward Jupiter.
beats.visual: Galileo spacecraft pre-launch preparation in clean room, 1989.

beats.text: Since its discovery in 1916, astronomers saw Gaspra as nothing more than a tiny point of light.
beats.visual: Telescope view showing asteroid Gaspra as a speck among stars.

beats.text: Galileo closed the gap, snapping fifty-seven images from as close as 3,300 miles away.
beats.visual: Galileo 11-image approach montage showing Gaspra's rotation, 1991.

beats.text: The resolution revealed details just 54 meters wide, showing a jagged world lacking large impact craters.
beats.visual: Highest resolution two-image mosaic of asteroid 951 Gaspra taken by Galileo, 1991.

beats.text: But the biggest shock was the linear grooves, which had previously only been seen on the Martian moon Phobos.
beats.visual: Comparison montage of asteroid Gaspra and Martian moon Phobos showing surface grooves.

beats.text: These fractures suggest Gaspra was born from the violent, catastrophic breakup of a much larger parent asteroid.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of an asteroid collision and breakup.

beats.text: It was the first time humanity saw the scars carved into a deep-space rock.
beats.visual: False color mosaic of asteroid Gaspra highlighting surface variations, Galileo, 1991.
